title: LINQ basics
summary: Filter, transform, sort and pick items from any collection with a chain of small method calls.

steps.title: Where and Select
body: In the last lesson you wrote `Filter` and `Map`. .NET ships them for every collection, under the names **`Where`** and **`Select`**. They are part of **LINQ** (Language Integrated Query).
```csharp
record Employee(string Name, string Dept, int Salary, int Years);
List<string> itNames = employees
.Where(e => e.Dept == "IT")      // keep the ones that pass the test
.Select(e => e.Name)             // turn each one into something else
.ToList();                       // collect the results into a List
- Each call takes a lambda and returns a new sequence, so calls **chain**. Read the chain top to bottom.
- The original collection is never changed.
- The result of `Where` or `Select` is an `IEnumerable<T>`: something you can `foreach` over. Call `ToList()` or `ToArray()` when you need a real list or array.
LINQ works on arrays, `List<T>`, `Dictionary`, `HashSet`, strings: anything you can loop over.

steps.explain: `Where` keeps 12, 8 and 20, in their original order. `Select` then multiplies each of those by 10.

steps.prompt: Complete the query so `names` holds the name of every employee in the Sales department.
steps.explain: `Where` filters, `Select` transforms, `ToList` turns the result into a `List<string>`.

steps.title: Senior staff
prompt: record Employee(string Name, string Dept, int Salary, int Years);
Write `static List<string> SeniorNames(List<Employee> staff, int minYears)`. It returns the **names** of everyone who has worked at least `minYears` years, in the order they appear in `staff`.
starter: static List<string> SeniorNames(List<Employee> staff, int minYears)
// one chain: filter, then pick the name, then ToList
solution: static List<string> SeniorNames(List<Employee> staff, int minYears)

Dojo.Eq("SeniorNames(staff, 3) also includes Flo", new List<string> { "Ann", "Cy", "Di", "Flo" }, SeniorNames(staff, 3));

hints: Start with `staff.Where(e => ...)`. The lambda can use the parameter `minYears`: that is a closure.
After the `Where`, add `.Select(e => e.Name)` to go from employees to strings.

steps.title: Sorting
body: `OrderBy` sorts by whatever the lambda returns. `OrderByDescending` sorts the other way.
```csharp
var byPay = employees.OrderByDescending(e => e.Salary);
To break ties, follow it with `ThenBy` or `ThenByDescending`:
```csharp
var roster = employees
.OrderBy(e => e.Dept)                 // first by department, A to Z
.ThenByDescending(e => e.Salary);     // inside a department, highest pay first
> **Tip:** Do not call `OrderBy` twice. The second call throws away the first sort and starts again. `ThenBy` keeps it.
The lambda only says *what to sort by*. You never write a comparison yourself.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into one query: the names of the people in Sales, highest paid first.
steps.explain: `Select(e => e.Name)` has to come after the sort: once you only have names, there is no `Salary` left to sort by. `ToList()` comes last because it ends the chain. Filtering before sorting is the better habit: there is less to sort.

steps.title: Picking and asking
body: Some LINQ methods return **one item** or a **yes/no answer** instead of a sequence.
```csharp
Employee first  = employees.First(e => e.Dept == "IT");            // throws if there is none
Employee? maybe = employees.FirstOrDefault(e => e.Dept == "Legal"); // null if there is none
bool anyNew  = employees.Any(e => e.Years < 1);       // is there at least one?
bool allPaid = employees.All(e => e.Salary > 0);      // does every one pass?
Use `First` when a missing item is a bug. Use `FirstOrDefault` when "not found" is a normal answer, and then check for `null`. (For value types such as `int`, the default is `0`, not `null`.)
`Take` and `Skip` cut a sequence by position:
```csharp
var topThree = byPay.Take(3);            // the first three
var page2 = roster.Skip(10).Take(10);    // skip one page of ten, take the next
`Take` never throws. If there are fewer items than you ask for, you get what there is.

steps.prompt: `empty` is a `List<string>` with nothing in it. Match each call to what happens.
steps.explain: `All` on an empty sequence is `true`: no item fails the test. `Any()` with no lambda simply asks "is there anything in here?".

steps.prompt: `Enumerable.Range(1, 10)` is the sequence 1, 2, ... 10. What does this print?
steps.explain: `Skip(3)` drops 1, 2, 3. `Take(4)` keeps the next four: 4, 5, 6, 7. None of them is above 7, and all of them are above 3.

steps.title: Query syntax
body: Everything so far is **method syntax**. C# also has **query syntax**, which looks a little like SQL:
```csharp
var names = from e in employees
where e.Salary > 50000
orderby e.Name
select e.Name;
The compiler rewrites it into exactly the method calls you already know:
```csharp
var names = employees
.Where(e => e.Salary > 50000)
.OrderBy(e => e.Name)
.Select(e => e.Name);
Neither is faster. Most C# code uses method syntax, and many methods (`Take`, `Any`, `First`, ...) have no query keyword. You should be able to *read* query syntax; this course writes method syntax.

steps.prompt: Which method chain does the same as this query?
code: var result = from e in employees
steps.explain: `where` becomes `Where`, `orderby ... descending` becomes `OrderByDescending`, and `select` becomes `Select`, in the same order as the query.

steps.title: Staff directory
prompt: The harness defines `record Employee(string Name, string Dept, int Salary, int Years);`
Write three methods for a staff directory. No loops: each one is a single LINQ chain.
- `static List<string> RosterPage(List<Employee> staff, int page, int pageSize)`
Sort by `Dept` (A to Z), then by `Salary` (highest first). Return the **names** on the given page. `page` starts at 1. A page past the end is an empty list.
The highest-paid employee in `dept`, or `null` if nobody works there.
`true` when every employee has a `Salary` of `minimum` or more.
starter: static List<string> RosterPage(List<Employee> staff, int page, int pageSize)
static Employee? TopEarner(List<Employee> staff, string dept)
static bool AllEarnAtLeast(List<Employee> staff, int minimum)
solution: static List<string> RosterPage(List<Employee> staff, int page, int pageSize)
static Employee? TopEarner(List<Employee> staff, string dept)

Dojo.Eq("RosterPage(staff, 1, 2) is Ed, Cy", new List<string> { "Ed", "Cy" }, RosterPage(staff, 1, 2));
Dojo.Eq("RosterPage(staff, 2, 2) is Ann, Flo", new List<string> { "Ann", "Flo" }, RosterPage(staff, 2, 2));
Dojo.Eq("RosterPage(staff, 2, 4) is the last two: Di, Bo", new List<string> { "Di", "Bo" }, RosterPage(staff, 2, 4));
Dojo.Eq("RosterPage(staff, 4, 2) is empty", new List<string>(), RosterPage(staff, 4, 2));
Dojo.Check("TopEarner(staff, \"Legal\") is null", TopEarner(staff, "Legal") is null, "expected null because nobody works in Legal");
Dojo.Eq("the staff list itself is not re-sorted", "Ann", staff[0].Name);

hints: `RosterPage`: `OrderBy(e => e.Dept).ThenByDescending(e => e.Salary)`, then `Skip`, `Take`, `Select`, `ToList`. Page 1 skips nothing, page 2 skips `pageSize` items, so skip `(page - 1) * pageSize`.
`TopEarner`: filter to the department, sort by salary descending, then `FirstOrDefault()` gives the top one or `null`.
